Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: At fifty-four, Elena Morales still remembers the exact moment the desert floor gave way. She had been directing a demolition sequence for a road-clearing operation when a buried charge detonated prematurely. The blast threw her against the cab of her engineering vehicle, and for a fraction of a second, a searing wave of heat registered on her left forearm at precisely one hundred forty degrees. Before she could process the burn, the air filled with the sharp, overlapping shouts of her crew as the dust cloud swallowed the clearing and the ground pitched beneath her boots. What followed was not a sequence of events she could piece together, only a fractured impression of collapsing metal and the smell of burning cordite. She walked away with bruised ribs and a hollow chest, but the memory refused to settle into a straight line. Even now, she cannot recount what happened without losing her place, unable to trace a beginning, middle, or end, her mind refusing to hold a coherent story even when she tries to speak it aloud. Over the next several months, her body refused to stand down. Elena found herself perpetually coiled, every muscle braced as though another detonation were minutes away. This constant tension settled in her shoulders and made reading engineering schematics feel like wading through water. Her gaze constantly drifted to the periphery as she scanned every briefing room and corridor for concealed risks. When the base fell unusually quiet after a scheduled training exercise, the absence of noise made her stomach tighten; she was certain the quiet meant something dangerous was about to happen. To keep the dread at bay, she stopped engaging with her colleagues, retreating into a thick emotional numbness that allowed her to function without feeling the weight of the years. She avoided planning anything beyond the next twenty-four hours, sidestepping difficult conversations and complex operational reviews, convincing herself that keeping life simple was the only way to stay safe. Back in her home state, married for over twenty years, Elena's avoidance took root in her marriage. She stopped attending neighborhood gatherings and declined requests from her husband to tackle household repairs, fearing that any unstructured demand might unravel her composure. When a portable heater in the engineering depot flickered to life, the sudden visual of the flames made her step back from her workbench, her fingers stilling over the blueprint. The tactile memory of that precise heat on her skin returned instantly, and she walked out of the facility, telling herself she would return tomorrow. The avoidance hardened over time, leaving her superiors to note a gradual withdrawal from high-risk assignments. When a campfire lit up a neighbor's yard, the visual of the open fire made her drop her coffee mug, her breath catching as the temperature on her skin jumped to that exact same mark. Shouting from a nearby road construction site sent her backing into a wall, her heart hammering against her ribs. The world had become a place that could not be trusted, and when the memories surfaced without warning, sometimes she heard the cracked voices of her former sergeant echoing in the quiet of her own kitchen. She looked at herself in the mirror and felt a quiet certainty that something was fundamentally wrong with her, that she had been broken by an event that had gone entirely unpunished, leaving behind a deep sense of injustice. At fifty-four, the weight of the constant readiness finally outpaced her defenses. The breaking point came when she missed a critical engineering survey because she could not focus long enough to read the topographical maps, followed by a quiet but firm conversation with her husband who noted that they barely recognized each other. What frightened Elena most was the fear that she would lose the last fragments of control she had left, that the fractured memories would keep pulling her back into that heat and noise for the rest of her life. She sat in the waiting room that morning hoping for a way to unclench her muscles, to finally piece together what happened, and to stop bracing for a danger that had already passed.
